hypothesis: Across human growth, body weight scales approximately as the cube of stature (log-log slope near 3), and cubing the stature-versus-age curve removes most of the difference in shape between the stature curve and the weight curve.
pass_criterion: Pre-registered, on pooled NHANES 2007-2018 individuals aged 0-19.99 yr with measured weight and stature (recumbent length < 24 months, standing height >= 24 months), sexes pooled with sex-specific values reported. (1) Cube tendency: the OLS slope b of log10(weight) on log10(stature) over all individuals satisfies 2.5 <= b <= 3.5 (95% CI reported; reduced-major-axis slope reported as sensitivity), and the same slope fitted to the age-median curve (monthly median weight vs monthly median stature, 0-19 yr) also lies in [2.5, 3.5]. (2) 'Mainly explains the curve difference': with monthly medians H(t), W(t) normalised to their 19-yr values, define D(p) = mean over months of |W(t)/W(19) - (H(t)/H(19))^p|. Supports if D(3)/D(1) <= 0.5, i.e. cubing the stature curve removes at least half of the discrepancy between the stature and weight curves. Both (1) and (2) must hold for 'supports'.
fail_criterion: Refutes if the individual-level slope b lies outside [2.0, 4.0], or if D(3)/D(1) > 1 (cubing makes the curves less alike). Mixed if b is in [2.0, 2.5) or (3.5, 4.0], or if the slope is in range but 0.5 < D(3)/D(1) <= 1 (the cube explains some but not most of the difference).
interpretation: Thompson's 'linear dimension' is stature, 'weight' is body mass; 'tend to vary as the cube' is read as a log-log allometric exponent within 0.5 of 3 (his own hedge). The second half of the claim, that cubic scaling 'mainly (though not wholly)' explains why the weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve, is read as: the cube of the normalised stature curve is at least twice as close to the normalised weight curve as the stature curve itself. Humans only; the parenthetical extension to organisms generally is not tested. Cross-sectional data, modern US population.
